title: Arteries & Veins of the Head and Neck
summary: The full vascular map, from the carotids and vertebrals in the neck to venous drainage of the face and cranium.

lessons.title: Common Carotid Artery, Carotid Bifurcation, Sinus & Body

levels.kid:
Your heart pumps blood up to your head through two big tubes in your neck. They are called the **carotid arteries**, one on each side. Put two fingers gently beside your windpipe and you can feel one beating. That beat is your pulse!

Partway up your neck, each tube splits into two, like a road forking. One branch feeds your face. The other feeds your brain.

Right at the fork there are two tiny helpers. One is a stretchy spot that works like a pressure gauge. It tells your brain if your blood is pushing too hard. The other is a tiny lump the size of a grain of rice. It tastes your blood to check that it has enough oxygen.
levels.hs:
The **common carotid arteries (CCAs)** are the main blood supply to the head. They start differently on each side. The right one branches from the **brachiocephalic trunk**. The left one comes straight off the **aortic arch**.

Each CCA runs up the neck inside a tube of connective tissue called the **carotid sheath**. The sheath also holds the **internal jugular vein** and the **vagus nerve**. The CCA has no branches in the neck. At about the level of the upper border of the **thyroid cartilage** (Adam's apple), roughly vertebra C3-C4, it splits at the **carotid bifurcation** into:
- the **internal carotid artery**, mainly to the brain and eye
- the **external carotid artery**, to the face, scalp and neck

Two sensors sit at the bifurcation:
- The **carotid sinus** is a widening at the start of the internal carotid. Its wall holds **baroreceptors**, stretch sensors that detect blood pressure.
- The **carotid body** is a tiny cluster of cells in the fork. It is a **chemoreceptor** that senses low oxygen.

Real example: you can feel the carotid pulse just in front of the **sternocleidomastoid** muscle. Health workers check it during resuscitation because it is a large, central pulse that is easy to find.
levels.college:
**Origins and course.** The right CCA arises from the brachiocephalic trunk behind the right sternoclavicular joint. The left CCA arises directly from the aortic arch, so it has a short thoracic segment. Both ascend in the **carotid sheath**, a condensation of deep cervical fascia, with the internal jugular vein lateral and the vagus nerve posterior, between the two vessels.

**Relations in the neck:**
- Posterior: the transverse processes of the cervical vertebrae and the prevertebral muscles. The **carotid tubercle** (Chassaignac's tubercle) of C6 lets you compress the CCA against bone.
- Anteromedial: trachea, esophagus, thyroid gland and recurrent laryngeal nerve.
- Anterior: the sternocleidomastoid overlaps it. Above the omohyoid it lies in the **carotid triangle**, where it is most superficial. The **ansa cervicalis** usually sits on or in the sheath.

The CCA gives **no named branches** in the neck. It divides near the upper border of the thyroid cartilage (C3-C4), although the level varies from about C2 to C6. The ICA usually starts posterolateral to the ECA.

**Carotid sinus:** a dilation of the proximal ICA. It has a thinner media and a richer adventitial nerve supply. Stretch receptors signal through the **carotid sinus nerve (Hering's nerve)**, a branch of **CN IX**, to the **nucleus tractus solitarius**. A rise in pressure increases vagal output and reduces sympathetic tone, which slows the heart and dilates vessels. This is the **baroreflex**.

**Carotid body:** a small chemoreceptor in the bifurcation, supplied by ECA twigs and receiving very high blood flow. **Glomus (type I) cells** sense falling PaO2, rising PaCO2 and falling pH, and also signal via CN IX. The result is increased breathing.

Clinically, the bifurcation is the commonest site of **atherosclerotic plaque**, because flow there is disturbed.
levels.phd:
**Hemodynamics of the bulb.** The bifurcation is a classic site of complex flow. At the outer (posterolateral) wall of the carotid bulb, opposite the flow divider, flow separates and recirculates, and wall shear stress is low and oscillating. Ku, Giddens, Zarins and Glagov (1985) related plaque thickness to these conditions. Intimal thickening matched low, oscillatory shear rather than high shear. Endothelium under laminar high shear expresses KLF2/KLF4 and eNOS, which protect the vessel wall. Disturbed flow activates NF-kB, VCAM-1 and other pro-inflammatory programs, which predisposes the bulb to plaque.

**Baroreceptor transduction.** Afferent endings in the sinus adventitia sense the stretch of the wall, not pressure as such. **Piezo1 and Piezo2** are the key mechanotransducers. Zeng et al. (2018, Science) showed that deleting both abolishes the baroreflex. The afferent cell bodies sit in the **petrosal (inferior glossopharyngeal) ganglion** and project to the NTS. From there, signals reach the caudal ventrolateral medulla, which inhibits the RVLM and lowers sympathetic outflow, and the nucleus ambiguus, which increases cardiac vagal output. Baroreceptors reset to sustained hypertension within days, so they are considered short-term regulators. Whether the baroreflex helps control long-term blood pressure is still debated.

**Chemotransduction.** In glomus cells, hypoxia inhibits **O2-sensitive K+ channels** (TASK-like and others). This depolarizes the cells, opens voltage-gated Ca2+ channels and releases ATP and other transmitters onto petrosal afferents. Mitochondrial complex I and **Olfr78** (proposed lactate sensing) are the leading candidate oxygen sensors. The carotid body responds within seconds and is the main peripheral driver of hypoxic ventilation. The aortic bodies (via CN X) contribute much less in humans. Bilateral carotid body resection blunts the ventilatory response to hypoxia.

**Development.** The CCA comes from the **third pharyngeal arch artery** together with the proximal ICA. The ECA buds from the aortic sac region. The carotid body comes from neural crest cells, which explains its link to paragangliomas.
levels.expert:
**Imaging and anatomy for the surgeon.** On ultrasound the ECA can be identified because it has branches, lies anteromedial and has a high-resistance waveform. Tapping the superficial temporal artery transmits a pulse into it. The ICA has a low-resistance waveform. Doppler criteria from the Society of Radiologists in Ultrasound consensus (an ICA peak systolic velocity of about 125 cm/s or more suggests 50% stenosis or greater) are screening thresholds, not measurements. Stenosis is graded on CTA or MRA by the **NASCET** method, which uses the distal ICA as the denominator. The older ECST method gives higher stenosis percentages than NASCET.

**Endarterectomy (CEA).** NASCET and ECST showed clear benefit of surgery for symptomatic 70-99% stenosis, smaller benefit for 50-69%, and the greatest benefit when surgery happens within about two weeks of the event. Exposure is along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid. The facial vein is ligated to reach the bifurcation. Nerves at risk:
- **Hypoglossal nerve**, which crosses the ICA and ECA high in the field
- **Vagus nerve** and its recurrent laryngeal output
- **Superior laryngeal nerve**, which runs deep to the bifurcation
- **Marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve**, injured by retraction

A high bifurcation (C2 or above) makes exposure harder and favors stenting. For asymptomatic disease with modern medical therapy, the CREST-2 and ECST-2 trials are re-examining whether intervention helps.

**Sinus manipulation.** Dissection at the bulb can cause bradycardia and hypotension. Surgeons may infiltrate local anesthetic around the sinus nerve. After CEA or stenting, baroreflex dysfunction can cause unstable blood pressure. **Carotid sinus hypersensitivity** is a recognized cause of falls and fainting in older adults. Carotid sinus massage is avoided when there is a bruit or a recent stroke.

**Carotid body tumors** are paragangliomas that splay the ICA and ECA apart (the **lyre sign**). They are classified by the **Shamblin** system. They are linked to **SDHx** mutations, especially SDHD with its paternal inheritance pattern. Workup includes metanephrines and genetic testing, and embolization before surgery is debated. Device-based **baroreflex activation therapy** has FDA approval for some patients with heart failure. Whether carotid body ablation can treat hypertension is an open question.

keyPoints: Right CCA arises from the brachiocephalic trunk; left CCA arises from the aortic arch
CCA runs in the carotid sheath with the internal jugular vein and vagus nerve and has no neck branches
It bifurcates near the upper thyroid cartilage (about C3-C4) into the ICA and ECA
Carotid sinus: baroreceptors in the proximal ICA that signal blood pressure via CN IX
Carotid body: chemoreceptor glomus cells that sense low oxygen and drive breathing
Disturbed, low-shear flow makes the bifurcation a common site of atherosclerotic plaque

test.q: Where does the left common carotid artery arise?
test.explain: The left CCA comes straight off the aortic arch. The right CCA is the one that arises from the brachiocephalic trunk.

test.q: Which structures share the carotid sheath with the common carotid artery?
choices: External jugular vein and accessory nerve
Internal jugular vein and vagus nerve
test.explain: The carotid sheath holds the CCA, the internal jugular vein (lateral) and the vagus nerve (posterior, between the two vessels).

test.q: At about which landmark does the common carotid usually bifurcate?
choices: The angle of the mandible at C1
The upper thyroid cartilage at C3-C4
test.explain: The usual bifurcation level is the upper border of the thyroid cartilage, roughly C3-C4, although it varies.

test.q: How many named branches does the common carotid give off in the neck?
test.explain: The CCA gives no named branches in the neck. Its branches come only after it divides into the ICA and ECA.

test.q: The carotid sinus is a dilation of which vessel?
test.explain: The carotid sinus is a widening at the start of the internal carotid. Its wall contains baroreceptors.

test.q: What do the receptors of the carotid body mainly detect?
test.explain: The carotid body is a chemoreceptor that detects low PaO2, as well as high CO2 and low pH. Wall stretch is sensed by the carotid sinus instead.

test.q: Which cranial nerve carries signals from both the carotid sinus and the carotid body?
test.explain: The carotid sinus nerve (Hering's nerve) is a branch of CN IX and carries both baroreceptor and chemoreceptor signals.

test.q: What happens when blood pressure suddenly rises and the carotid sinus is stretched?
choices: Heart rate slows and vessels dilate
Heart rate rises and vessels constrict
Sympathetic tone rises to the heart
test.explain: The baroreflex increases vagal output and reduces sympathetic tone. This lowers heart rate and dilates vessels, bringing pressure back down.

test.q: Why does atherosclerotic plaque often form at the carotid bifurcation?
choices: Pressure from the thyroid on the vessel
Disturbed flow with low wall shear stress
High oxygen levels in the bulb blood
Thin outer adventitia across the bulb
test.explain: Flow separation at the bulb produces low, oscillating shear stress, which promotes inflammation of the vessel wall and plaque.

test.q: The right common carotid artery arises from the ___ trunk.
test.explain: The brachiocephalic trunk divides into the right subclavian and right common carotid arteries.

test.q: What general name is given to stretch sensors that detect blood pressure, like those in the carotid sinus?
test.explain: Baroreceptors sense how much the vessel wall is stretched by pressure.

test.q: The C6 carotid tubercle is also called ___'s tubercle.
test.explain: Chassaignac's tubercle on C6 lets the CCA be compressed against bone.

kidTest.q: What do the carotid arteries carry to your head?
kidTest.explain: The carotid arteries are big tubes that carry blood from the heart up to the head.

kidTest.q: What happens to each carotid tube partway up your neck?
kidTest.explain: Like a fork in the road, it splits into one branch for the face and one for the brain.

kidTest.q: The stretchy spot at the fork works like what?
kidTest.explain: It senses how hard the blood is pushing and tells the brain.

kidTest.q: What does the tiny lump at the fork check in your blood?
kidTest.explain: The carotid body checks that the blood has enough oxygen.

kidTest.q: You can feel the beat in your neck. That beat is your p _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: The beat you feel is your pulse, made by the heart pumping blood.

advancedTest.q: Ku and Glagov's work placed early plaque at the outer wall of the bulb, opposite the flow divider. What best explains this location?
choices: High laminar shear there overstretches and injures the endothelium
The outer wall receives fewer vasa vasorum and becomes ischemic
Baroreceptor nerve endings release inflammatory peptides at that site
Low, oscillating shear activates NF-kB instead of KLF2-driven protection
advancedTest.explain: Plaque matched low, oscillatory shear. High laminar shear is protective because it drives KLF2 and eNOS expression.

advancedTest.q: Mice lacking both Piezo1 and Piezo2 in baroreceptor neurons would most likely show:
choices: Normal baroreflex but absent carotid body firing
Exaggerated bradycardia during a rise in blood pressure
Loss of the hypoxic ventilatory response alone
Loss of baroreflex buffering, with labile blood pressure
advancedTest.explain: Piezo1/2 transduce wall stretch, and deleting both abolished the baroreflex. Hypoxia sensing by the carotid body works through a separate mechanism.

advancedTest.q: A carotid stenosis graded on CTA reads 72% by NASCET but higher by ECST. Why do the two methods differ?
choices: NASCET measures blood velocity, whereas ECST measures diameter
ECST compares the residual lumen with the estimated bulb diameter
NASCET corrects for ICA flow above the stenosis
ECST uses the common carotid lumen as its denominator
advancedTest.explain: Both methods measure the residual lumen at the tightest point, but they use different denominators. NASCET divides by the normal distal ICA diameter beyond the bulb. ECST divides by the estimated original diameter of the carotid bulb at the stenosis. The bulb is wider than the distal ICA, so the same residual lumen gives a higher ECST percentage; 70% by NASCET is roughly 85% by ECST. Using the common carotid as the reference is a separate method, not ECST.

advancedTest.q: Imaging shows a vascular neck mass that splays the ICA and ECA apart. What is the most appropriate genetic consideration?
choices: RET testing for medullary thyroid carcinoma
advancedTest.explain: The lyre sign points to a carotid body paraganglioma. These tumors are associated with SDHx mutations, especially SDHD.

lessons.title: Branches of the External Carotid Artery

levels.kid:
Your heart pumps blood up your neck through big tubes called **carotid arteries**. Near the top of your neck, each one splits in two, like a road splitting at a fork.

One road, the **internal carotid**, goes inside your skull to feed your brain. The other road, the **external carotid**, stays outside. It sends little side roads to your face, tongue, throat, scalp, ears and jaw.

There are eight main side roads. One goes to your tongue so it can move and taste. One curls around your jaw to your face. One runs up in front of your ear to your temple. You can feel it beating there!

Doctors learn this map so they know which road feeds which part of the head.
levels.hs:
The **common carotid artery** divides at about the level of the upper border of the thyroid cartilage (around the C3-C4 vertebrae). The **internal carotid artery (ICA)** has no branches in the neck and supplies the brain and eye. The **external carotid artery (ECA)** supplies almost everything else in the head and neck: face, scalp, tongue, throat, thyroid, jaw muscles, teeth and the dura (the tough covering of the brain).

The ECA has **eight branches**. A popular memory trick is "Some Anatomists Like Freaking Out Poor Medical Students":
- **S**uperior thyroid: thyroid gland and larynx
- **A**scending pharyngeal: throat wall
- **L**ingual: tongue
- **F**acial: face
- **O**ccipital: back of the scalp
- **P**osterior auricular: behind the ear
- **M**axillary: deep face, teeth, nose, dura
- **S**uperficial temporal: side of the scalp

The last two are **terminal branches**. The ECA ends inside the parotid salivary gland, behind the jaw, by splitting into them.

Real example: you can feel the **facial artery** pulse where it crosses the lower edge of your jaw, just in front of the chewing muscle (masseter). You can feel the **superficial temporal artery** pulse just in front of your ear. Because the branches on both sides connect with each other across the face, facial cuts bleed heavily but heal well.
levels.college:
The ECA begins at the carotid bifurcation and initially lies **anteromedial** to the ICA (a useful distinction on ultrasound and in surgery, along with the fact that the ECA branches and the ICA does not). It ascends through the carotid triangle, passes deep to the posterior belly of digastric and stylohyoid, and enters the **parotid gland**. Behind the neck of the mandible it divides into its terminal branches.

**Anterior branches**
- **Superior thyroid**: often the first branch. It descends to the thyroid upper pole and gives the **superior laryngeal artery**, which pierces the thyrohyoid membrane with the internal laryngeal nerve.
- **Lingual**: loops upward at the greater horn of the hyoid, then passes **deep to hyoglossus**. The hypoglossal nerve runs superficial to that muscle. It ends as the deep lingual artery.
- **Facial**: grooves the submandibular gland, hooks over the mandible at the anterior border of masseter, then winds tortuously toward the medial canthus as the **angular artery**. It gives ascending palatine, tonsillar (the main tonsil supply), submental, labial and lateral nasal branches.

**Medial branch**
- **Ascending pharyngeal**: a small branch from the deep surface supplying the pharynx, prevertebral muscles, middle ear and meninges.

**Posterior branches**
- **Occipital**: runs along the lower border of the posterior belly of digastric, crossed by the hypoglossal nerve, to the posterior scalp.
- **Posterior auricular**: supplies the auricle and scalp; its stylomastoid branch feeds the facial nerve canal.

**Terminal branches**
- **Superficial temporal**: crosses the zygomatic arch in front of the tragus, alongside the auriculotemporal nerve.
- **Maxillary**: passes deep to the mandibular neck into the infratemporal and pterygopalatine fossae.

Origins vary. Linguofacial trunks occur in roughly 10-20% of people.
levels.phd:
The **maxillary artery** is divided by its relation to the lateral pterygoid into three parts.

- **First (mandibular) part**: deep auricular, anterior tympanic, **middle meningeal**, accessory meningeal and inferior alveolar arteries. The middle meningeal artery ascends between the two roots of the auriculotemporal nerve and enters the skull through the **foramen spinosum**. The inferior alveolar artery enters the mandibular foramen.
- **Second (pterygoid) part**: masseteric, deep temporal, pterygoid and buccal arteries.
- **Third (pterygopalatine) part**: posterior superior alveolar, infraorbital, descending palatine (greater and lesser palatine), artery of the pterygoid canal, pharyngeal and **sphenopalatine** arteries. The sphenopalatine artery enters the nasal cavity through the sphenopalatine foramen.

**Developmental basis.** The ECA arises as a ventral sprout from the third arch region. It annexes the territory of the regressing stapedial artery, a second-arch derivative whose distal divisions become the middle meningeal, infraorbital and inferior alveolar territories. This explains rare anomalies, such as a **persistent stapedial artery** traversing the stapes footplate with absence of the foramen spinosum, or an ophthalmic origin of the middle meningeal artery.

**Ascending pharyngeal artery.** Its neuromeningeal trunk sends branches through the hypoglossal canal and jugular foramen. It supplies cranial nerves IX-XII and the posterior fossa dura. It is a key feeder of jugulotympanic paragangliomas and many dural arteriovenous fistulas.

**Anastomotic network.** The ECA anastomoses extensively:
- across the midline with the opposite ECA (labial, lingual, thyroid arcades)
- with the ICA via angular-dorsal nasal, middle meningeal-ophthalmic (recurrent meningeal) and inferolateral trunk connections, and the artery of the pterygoid canal
- with the vertebral artery via occipital-muscular branches

In ICA occlusion, retrograde flow through the ophthalmic artery can sustain intracranial perfusion. Ligating the ECA rarely causes ischemia because of this redundancy. For the same reason it only modestly reduces distal bleeding, as Burnham-era ligation series and later physiological work showed.
levels.expert:
For the clinician, ECA anatomy matters most in hemorrhage control, tumor embolization, revascularization and endovascular safety.

**Epistaxis.** About 90% of nosebleeds arise anteriorly in Kiesselbach's plexus (Little's area). Refractory posterior bleeding is usually sphenopalatine. **Endoscopic sphenopalatine artery ligation** has largely replaced proximal ECA ligation, with reported success above 85-90%. Look for the **crista ethmoidalis**, which marks the foramen, and expect multiple branches. Combine it with anterior ethmoidal ligation (an ICA territory) when bleeding is superior.

**Dangerous anastomoses.** During embolization of meningiomas, juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibromas, paragangliomas or dural AV fistulas, liquid agents or small particles can reflux into the ICA or vertebral artery, or block vasa nervorum.
- The petrous branch of the middle meningeal artery supplies the facial nerve, so occluding it risks facial palsy.
- The neuromeningeal trunk of the ascending pharyngeal artery supplies the lower cranial nerves.
- Occipital-vertebral anastomoses at C1-C2 can carry emboli to the posterior circulation.

Superselective angiography with provocative testing, and careful choice of particle size, reduce these risks. Middle meningeal artery embolization for chronic subdural hematoma (EMBOLISE, MAGIC-MT and STEM trials, published 2024) cut recurrence and reoperation after surgical evacuation. This made the ECA an active neurosurgical target.

**Bypass donors.** The superficial temporal artery serves low-flow STA-MCA bypass for moyamoya and selected occlusive disease. The occipital artery is used for posterior circulation bypass (OA-PICA). Preserve both branches of the STA when planning scalp incisions such as pterional and bicoronal flaps; injuring the STA risks flap ischemia and loss of a future donor.

**Pitfalls.**
- **Giant cell arteritis** classically involves the superficial temporal artery. Biopsy can miss skip lesions; ultrasound showing a "halo sign" is increasingly accepted.
- Iatrogenic injury to the STA or middle meningeal artery can produce pseudoaneurysms or traumatic AV fistulas.
- On Doppler ultrasound, a temporal tap transmitting into the waveform identifies the ECA.

**Open questions.** How best to select chronic subdural patients for embolization (standalone or adjunctive) is still uncertain.

keyPoints: The ECA supplies most of the head and neck outside the skull, plus the dura
Eight branches: superior thyroid, ascending pharyngeal, lingual, facial, occipital, posterior auricular, maxillary, superficial temporal
The ECA ends in the parotid gland as the maxillary and superficial temporal arteries
The middle meningeal artery (from the maxillary) enters the skull via the foramen spinosum
The sphenopalatine artery is the main source of posterior nosebleeds
Rich anastomoses with the ICA and vertebral artery create embolization risks and backup flow routes

test.q: How many named branches does the external carotid artery classically have?
test.explain: Eight, remembered with 'Some Anatomists Like Freaking Out Poor Medical Students'.

test.q: Inside which structure does the ECA divide into its terminal branches?
test.explain: The ECA enters the parotid gland and divides behind the mandibular neck.

test.q: Which pair forms the terminal branches of the ECA?
test.explain: The maxillary and superficial temporal arteries are the two terminal branches.

test.q: Where can you feel the facial artery pulse?
choices: At the medial end of the eyebrow
Lower jaw edge, in front of masseter
Just in front of the ear's tragus
Behind the angle of the jaw
test.explain: It hooks over the mandible at the anterior border of masseter. The pulse in front of the tragus is the superficial temporal.

test.q: The lingual artery passes deep to which muscle?
test.explain: It runs deep to hyoglossus, while the hypoglossal nerve lies superficial to that muscle.

test.q: Which branch gives off the superior laryngeal artery?
test.explain: The superior thyroid artery gives the superior laryngeal artery, which pierces the thyrohyoid membrane.

test.q: Which artery is the main supply of the palatine tonsil?
test.explain: The tonsillar branch of the facial artery is the main tonsil supply.

test.q: How is the ECA told apart from the ICA in the neck?
choices: It is wider at its origin
It has no branches in the neck
It has branches in the neck
It lies posterolateral to the ICA
test.explain: The ECA branches in the neck and lies anteromedially at first. The ICA gives no neck branches.

test.q: Which branch runs along the lower border of the posterior belly of digastric?
test.explain: The occipital artery follows this border and is crossed by the hypoglossal nerve.

test.q: Through which foramen does the middle meningeal artery enter the skull?
test.explain: The middle meningeal artery, from the first part of the maxillary artery, enters through the foramen spinosum.

test.q: Near the medial corner of the eye, the facial artery ends as the ___ artery.
test.explain: The angular artery anastomoses with the dorsal nasal branch of the ophthalmic artery.

test.q: Which artery, a branch of the maxillary, is the main source of posterior nosebleeds?
test.explain: The sphenopalatine artery enters the nose via the sphenopalatine foramen and is targeted for refractory posterior epistaxis.

kidTest.q: Where does the external carotid artery send blood?
kidTest.explain: It feeds the outside parts of the head and the neck.

kidTest.q: Which carotid goes inside the skull to the brain?
kidTest.explain: The internal carotid goes inside to feed the brain.

kidTest.q: Where can you feel a pulse from a side road of the external carotid?
choices: In the middle of your back
kidTest.explain: The superficial temporal artery beats just in front of your ear.

kidTest.q: How many main side roads does the external carotid have?
kidTest.explain: It has eight main branches.

kidTest.q: One side road feeds your t _ _ _ _ _ so it can move and taste.
kidTest.explain: The lingual artery supplies the tongue.

advancedTest.q: Particle embolization of the middle meningeal artery near its petrous branch risks which deficit?
choices: Loss of hearing from cochlear ischemia
advancedTest.explain: The petrous branch supplies the facial nerve, so occluding it risks facial palsy.

advancedTest.q: Why does proximal ECA ligation often fail to stop posterior epistaxis?
choices: Posterior bleeds come mostly from the veins
The sphenopalatine artery arises from the ICA
The ECA has no branches above the parotid
advancedTest.explain: Rich side-to-side and ECA-ICA anastomoses restore distal flow. This is why distal sphenopalatine ligation works better.

advancedTest.q: An absent foramen spinosum with an artery crossing the stapes most likely reflects:
choices: Persistence of the embryonic stapedial artery
Agenesis of the external carotid artery
Duplication of the ascending pharyngeal artery
An aberrant origin of the occipital artery
advancedTest.explain: The middle meningeal territory normally comes from the regressing stapedial artery. If that artery persists, the middle meningeal artery may be missing from the foramen spinosum.

advancedTest.q: With a complete ICA occlusion, which ECA pathway can sustain flow into the ICA territory?
choices: Lingual to the deep lingual artery
Facial and angular, retrograde via the ophthalmic
Superior thyroid to the inferior thyroid
Posterior auricular to the stylomastoid branch
advancedTest.explain: Angular-dorsal nasal connections allow reversed ophthalmic flow into the intracranial ICA.

lessons.title: Segments of the Internal Carotid Artery from Neck to Brain

levels.kid:
Your brain is very hungry. It needs lots of blood all the time. Two big pipes in your neck, one on each side, carry much of that blood up. Each one is called the **internal carotid artery**.

This pipe takes an amazing trip. It climbs up your neck with no side branches. Then it squeezes through a tunnel in the skull bone. It bends like a twisty slide. It passes through a soft pool of blood next to your eye. Finally it pops up beside the brain and splits into branches that feed the front parts of your brain and your eye.

Doctors give each part of the trip a number, like stops on a train line. That helps them talk about exactly where a problem is.
levels.hs:
The **internal carotid artery (ICA)** is one of two main supply lines to the brain. It starts in the neck where the common carotid artery splits, at about the level of the top of the **thyroid cartilage** (the C3-C4 vertebrae). The ICA then travels up to the skull base. Along the way it gives off **no branches in the neck**, which is one way surgeons tell it apart from the external carotid.

Because its path is long and twisty, anatomists divide it into **segments**. The most widely used system, from **Bouthillier** and colleagues in 1996, names seven, labeled C1 to C7 in the direction blood flows:
- **C1 cervical**: in the neck
- **C2 petrous**: inside the dense temporal bone, in the carotid canal
- **C3 lacerum**: over the foramen lacerum
- **C4 cavernous**: inside the cavernous sinus, a pool of venous blood beside the pituitary gland
- **C5 clinoid**: a short piece near a bony point called the anterior clinoid process
- **C6 ophthalmic**: gives off the artery to the eye
- **C7 communicating**: ends by splitting into the **anterior** and **middle cerebral arteries**

Real example: an **aneurysm** (a weak, ballooning spot) often forms where the ICA gives off branches, such as the posterior communicating artery. Naming the segment tells a neurosurgeon where to look.
levels.college:
The ICA begins at the carotid bifurcation and ends at the terminal split into the anterior cerebral artery (ACA) and middle cerebral artery (MCA). The Bouthillier (1996) classification numbers segments C1-C7 in the direction of flow:

- **C1 cervical**: runs in the carotid sheath with the internal jugular vein (lateral) and vagus nerve (posterior). It starts posterolateral to the external carotid and passes deep to the posterior belly of digastric and the styloid muscles, with the pharynx medial to it. It has no branches. The **carotid bulb** at its origin holds the baroreceptive carotid sinus.
- **C2 petrous**: enters the carotid canal and runs vertically, then turns at a genu to run anteromedially. It is close to the cochlea and middle ear, separated from the tympanic cavity by thin bone. Small branches include the **caroticotympanic artery** and the **vidian artery** (artery of the pterygoid canal).
- **C3 lacerum**: lies above the cartilage-filled foramen lacerum. It does not pass through it. The segment ends at the petrolingual ligament.
- **C4 cavernous**: runs in the cavernous sinus with the **abducens nerve (CN VI)** lateral to it. CN III, IV, V1 and V2 lie in the lateral wall. Branches are the **meningohypophyseal trunk** and the **inferolateral trunk**.
- **C5 clinoid**: a short wedge between the proximal and distal dural rings.
- **C6 ophthalmic**: intradural. It gives the **ophthalmic artery** and **superior hypophyseal arteries**.
- **C7 communicating**: gives the **posterior communicating** and **anterior choroidal arteries**, then bifurcates.

C4 through C6 together form the S-shaped **carotid siphon** seen on angiograms. Segments C1-C5 are extradural. The distal dural ring marks entry into the subarachnoid space, so a rupture beyond it bleeds into the subarachnoid space.
levels.phd:
Several segmental schemes exist. **Fischer (1938)** numbered segments C1-C5 *against* flow, based on angiographic appearance. **Gibo and Rhoton (1981)** described four microsurgical parts: cervical, petrous, cavernous and supraclinoid. **Bouthillier, van Loveren and Keller (1996)** added the lacerum and clinoid segments and numbered with flow. **Ziyal**, and later endoscopic endonasal groups such as **Labib and colleagues (2014)**, refined the paraclival and parasellar portions for ventral approaches, because their surgical corridors differ. These systems use conflicting numbers. Unless a scheme is named, writing "C2" in a note can be ambiguous.

The clinoid segment is the main point of controversy. The **proximal dural ring**, formed by periosteum under the anterior clinoid process, is often incomplete. The **distal dural ring**, formed by dura over the clinoid, is usually complete laterally but thin medially. The **carotid cave** is a small recess of subarachnoid space medial to the clinoid ICA. Aneurysms there may be intradural despite looking paraclinoid. Getting this boundary right decides whether an aneurysm can cause subarachnoid hemorrhage, and so whether it needs treatment.

Embryologically, the ICA comes from the **third aortic arch** proximally and the **dorsal aorta** distally. Leftover embryonic channels explain several variants:
- **Persistent trigeminal artery**, about 0.1-0.6% of people: a carotid-basilar link at the cavernous segment
- **Aberrant ICA** in the middle ear: the ICA comes through the inferior tympanic canaliculus and looks like a retrotympanic mass
- **Persistent stapedial artery**

The vidian and inferolateral trunk anastomoses with external carotid branches form collateral routes. They matter during occlusion and can be dangerous during embolization.

Hemodynamically, tortuosity and curves at the siphon concentrate wall shear stress at the outer curvatures and at branch points. This fits the clustering of aneurysms at the ophthalmic, superior hypophyseal and posterior communicating origins.
levels.expert:
Clinically, each segment has its own disease profile.

**Cervical segment.** Atherosclerosis clusters at the bulb. In symptomatic high-grade stenosis, carotid endarterectomy outperforms medical therapy. NASCET used the narrowest residual lumen relative to the distal normal ICA. **Dissection** is a leading cause of stroke in young adults. It typically begins about 2 cm above the bifurcation and ends before the petrous canal. Its classic signs are ipsilateral Horner syndrome (from the sympathetic plexus on the artery), neck pain and lower cranial nerve palsies. Fibromuscular dysplasia and coiling or kinking also involve this segment. During high cervical exposure, watch for the hypoglossal nerve crossing superficially and, higher up, the glossopharyngeal nerve.

**Petrous and lacerum segments.** These matter in skull base fractures, in petrous apex lesions, and as the landmark for the anterior petrosectomy (Kawase). Middle fossa drilling exposes the horizontal petrous ICA medial to the greater petrosal nerve, and sometimes the bony roof over it is missing. **Endoscopic endonasal** work uses the vidian canal to locate the lacerum genu. ICA injury is the most feared complication of these approaches. Packing, endovascular sacrifice after balloon test occlusion, or covered stents are the rescue options.

**Cavernous segment.** A direct **carotid-cavernous fistula** after trauma causes pulsatile proptosis, chemosis, a bruit and a CN VI palsy. Treatment is transarterial coiling or flow diversion. Cavernous aneurysms rarely cause subarachnoid hemorrhage but can compress nerves or rupture into the sinus.

**Paraclinoid and supraclinoid segments.** Clipping often requires extradural or intradural **anterior clinoidectomy** and proximal control in the neck. **Flow diverters** (the Pipeline device, approved in 2011) have changed how large paraclinoid aneurysms are managed. Anterior choroidal sacrifice risks an internal capsule infarct, so it must be preserved. A fetal-pattern posterior communicating artery makes the posterior circulation depend on the ICA.

Pitfalls: reporting a segment number without naming the classification; mistaking an infundibulum (under 3 mm, with the vessel arising from its apex) for a posterior communicating aneurysm; and failing to recognize an aberrant middle-ear ICA before myringotomy. Open questions include rupture risk in small paraclinoid lesions and how best to manage carotid webs.

keyPoints: The ICA starts at the carotid bifurcation (about C3-C4) and has no branches in the neck
Bouthillier numbers 7 segments with flow: cervical, petrous, lacerum, cavernous, clinoid, ophthalmic, communicating
The cavernous ICA has CN VI lateral to it; CN III, IV, V1 and V2 lie in the sinus wall
The distal dural ring marks where the ICA becomes intradural (subarachnoid)
C6 gives the ophthalmic artery; C7 gives PComm and anterior choroidal, then splits into ACA and MCA
Aneurysms, dissections and fistulas cluster at specific segments

To show where a problem is

Bouthillier did not assign numbers to the petrous part
C2 refers to a vertebra, not an arterial segment
Fischer numbered against flow, so C2 differs by scheme

It reliably causes an early abducens palsy
It may be intradural and capable of subarachnoid hemorrhage
It sits in the petrous canal, so it threatens hearing alone

Petrous fracture compressing the vidian artery
Bulb atheroma producing a carotid-cavernous fistula

They are the main supply to the cochlea

lessons.title: The Vertebral Artery: Course from Subclavian to Foramen Magnum

levels.kid:
Your brain needs lots of blood, so it gets it from four big pipes. Two pipes run up the front of your neck. Two more, called the **vertebral arteries**, sneak up the back.

Each vertebral artery starts near your shoulder, from an artery called the subclavian. Then it does something clever. It climbs through a row of little holes in the bones of your neck, like a train going through tunnels in a mountain. The bones protect it.

At the top, near your skull, it makes a twisty loop so it can bend when you turn your head. Then it slips into your skull through a big hole at the bottom. There, the two vertebral arteries join into one pipe that feeds the back of your brain.
levels.hs:
The **vertebral arteries** are a pair of arteries that supply the back of the brain, the brainstem and the cerebellum, along with the upper spinal cord. Together with the two internal carotid arteries, they make up the four main vessels feeding the brain. The vertebral pair supplies the **posterior circulation**.

Anatomists divide each vertebral artery's path into four parts, called **V1 to V4**:
- **V1**: it arises from the **subclavian artery**, the large artery heading toward the arm, and runs up to the neck bones.
- **V2**: it climbs through the **transverse foramina**, small holes in the side parts of the neck vertebrae. Usually it enters at the sixth cervical vertebra (C6) and goes up to C2.
- **V3**: it leaves the top vertebra (the **atlas**, C1), loops sideways and backward over it, and pierces the tough membrane covering the spinal cord.
- **V4**: it enters the skull through the **foramen magnum**. There the left and right vertebral arteries join to form the **basilar artery**.

The loop in V3 gives slack so the artery isn't stretched when you turn your head. One real example of why this matters: a sudden, forceful neck twist can tear the inner lining of the artery. This is called a **dissection**, and it can cause a stroke in the back of the brain.
levels.college:
The vertebral artery (VA) is usually the **first branch of the subclavian artery**. It arises from the subclavian's superior posterior aspect, medial to the anterior scalene. In about 5% of people the left VA arises directly from the **aortic arch**, between the left common carotid and left subclavian. Such an arch origin usually enters the transverse foramen at a higher level, often C5 or C4.

**V1 (pre-foraminal)**: ascends posterosuperiorly between longus colli and anterior scalene. It passes behind the common carotid artery and vertebral vein, and the inferior thyroid artery crosses in front of it. It lies in front of the C7 transverse process, the ventral rami of C7 and C8, and the sympathetic trunk. The cervicothoracic (stellate) ganglion lies close behind its origin.

**V2 (foraminal)**: in about 90% of people it enters the **C6 transverse foramen**. The C7 foramen usually carries only veins. It then ascends through the foramina of C6 to C2, surrounded by a venous plexus and sympathetic fibers. The cervical spinal nerves lie just behind it. Along the way it gives **spinal (radicular) branches** and muscular branches. At C2 it turns laterally to reach the more laterally placed C1 foramen.

**V3 (extradural, suboccipital)**: it leaves the C1 transverse foramen and curves posteromedially behind the lateral mass of the atlas. It lies in the **groove for the vertebral artery** on C1's posterior arch, within the **suboccipital triangle**. The C1 nerve (suboccipital nerve) lies between the artery and the bone. It then passes under the edge of the posterior atlanto-occipital membrane.

**V4 (intradural)**: it pierces the dura and arachnoid, ascends through the foramen magnum anterior to the medulla, and gives branches:
- the anterior and posterior spinal arteries
- the **posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA)**, its largest branch
- meningeal branches

At the pontomedullary junction the two VAs unite to form the **basilar artery**.

The VAs are often unequal in size. The left is **dominant** in roughly half of people.
levels.phd:
**Development.** The VA forms by **longitudinal anastomoses** between the cervical intersegmental arteries 1 to 6, followed by regression of their connections to the dorsal aorta. The seventh intersegmental artery persists as the proximal subclavian and gives the VA origin. Variations follow directly from this sequence:
- **Arch origin**, where the left VA comes off the arch rather than the subclavian.
- **Duplication or fenestration**, from persistence of two parallel channels.
- An **extraforaminal V3 course** below C1 (for example, an artery entering the canal between C1 and C2), from persistence of the first intersegmental artery.
- The **proatlantal intersegmental artery** (types I and II), a fetal carotid-vertebral anastomosis that can persist and supply the posterior circulation when the VA is hypoplastic.

**Hemodynamics and asymmetry.** VA diameter is commonly about 3 to 5 mm. Left dominance occurs in roughly 50%, right in about 25%, and the two are codominant in about 25%. **Hypoplasia** (diameter under about 2 mm) is found in about 10% of people. A hypoplastic VA may end in PICA, the so-called PICA termination, and contribute little to the basilar. Asymmetry matters because the basilar's flow can depend on one VA. It is also linked to vertebrobasilar ischemia and to basilar curvature toward the non-dominant side.

**V3 biomechanics.** The redundant suboccipital loop accommodates atlanto-axial rotation; C1–C2 supplies about half of cervical rotation. Rotation still stretches the contralateral VA. Cadaveric and Doppler studies show flow reduction at extreme rotation, the basis of **rotational vertebral artery occlusion (bow hunter syndrome)**. **Ponticulus posticus**, a bony bridge converting the C1 groove into the arcuate foramen, occurs in roughly 10–15% of people. It is debated as a contributor to compression.

**Dissection.** Extracranial VA dissection clusters at **V3** (and V2/V3 junction), where the mobile artery meets fixation points. Proposed triggers include minor trauma and neck manipulation, but the causal link remains contested because prodromal neck pain may itself prompt manipulation. Underlying arteriopathies (for example, fibromuscular dysplasia) and connective tissue disorders can predispose.

**Collateral networks.** V2 radicular branches anastomose with ascending and deep cervical arteries. Occipital artery muscular branches connect with VA branches at V3. These external carotid–vertebral links are the route for **dangerous anastomoses** in embolization.
levels.expert:
**Neurosurgical exposure of V3.** In far-lateral and suboccipital approaches, V3 is at risk during dissection over the C1 posterior arch. A standard working margin is to stay within about 1.5 cm of midline on the C1 posterior arch when stripping muscle, because the groove lies laterally. In children the safe margin is smaller. The **suboccipital cavernous sinus**, a venous plexus around V3, bleeds briskly and is controlled with hemostatic agents rather than coagulating near the artery. Ponticulus posticus can mimic a broad posterior arch. An unrecognized one can lead a surgeon to place a C1 lateral mass screw entry through it and endanger the VA. A CT reviewed preoperatively avoids this.

**Instrumentation.** C1–C2 transarticular and C2 pedicle screws risk VA injury when there is a **high-riding vertebral artery**, an enlarged groove eroding the C2 isthmus. This is reported in roughly 15–20% of patients undergoing C1–C2 fixation. Preoperative CT angiography to map the V2/V3 course is standard of care for upper cervical instrumentation. If one VA is injured, the decision whether to sacrifice it depends on whether the contralateral VA is dominant. Injury on the dominant side can cause catastrophic posterior circulation stroke.

**Endovascular pitfalls.** Origin (V1) stenosis is common in atherosclerosis. It is treated by stenting when symptomatic despite medical therapy, but restenosis rates are high. VAST and VIST trials showed no clear benefit over best medical therapy for many patients. When embolizing external carotid branches, especially the occipital and ascending pharyngeal arteries, unrecognized EC–VA anastomoses can carry particles into the posterior circulation.

**Imaging.** In **subclavian steal**, proximal subclavian stenosis reverses flow in the ipsilateral VA. Doppler shows retrograde or alternating flow. The phenomenon is often asymptomatic.

**Open questions.** Whether antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy is better for cervical artery dissection remains unresolved; CADISS and TREAT-CAD found no robust superiority. Dynamic imaging to diagnose bow hunter syndrome lacks standardized criteria. How best to manage asymptomatic hypoplasia in patients undergoing contralateral procedures also remains uncertain.

keyPoints: Vertebral arteries supply the posterior circulation: brainstem, cerebellum, occipital lobes
Usually the first branch of the subclavian; left arises from the arch in about 5%
Four segments: V1 pre-foraminal, V2 foraminal (C6 to C2), V3 suboccipital loop, V4 intradural
V3 lies in the C1 groove within the suboccipital triangle, giving slack for head rotation
V4 enters via foramen magnum, gives PICA, and joins its partner to form the basilar
Asymmetry, dissection at V3 and high-riding VA matter clinically and surgically

lessons.title: Facial, Jugular & Emissary Veins and Links to the Dural Sinuses

levels.kid:
Arteries carry fresh blood up to your head. Veins carry used blood back down to your heart. Think of them as roads going home.

The biggest road out of your head is the **jugular vein** in your neck. Inside your skull, blood collects in special tunnels called **sinuses**, made of tough brain covering. These tunnels empty into the jugular.

Here is a surprise. Some tiny veins poke right through holes in your skull. They connect the veins on your face and scalp to the tunnels inside. Doctors call them **emissary veins**.

Most face veins have no little doors to stop blood going backward. So a germ from a pimple near your nose can travel inside. That is why doctors take face infections seriously.
levels.hs:
Blood leaves the head through **veins**, which return it to the heart. Most cerebral blood drains through the **dural venous sinuses**. These are channels between two layers of the dura mater, the tough outer covering of the brain.

The main pathway:
- The sinuses meet at the back of the skull and flow through the **sigmoid sinus** into the **internal jugular vein (IJV)**.
- The IJV leaves the skull through the **jugular foramen** and runs down the neck inside the carotid sheath.
- It joins the subclavian vein to form the **brachiocephalic vein**, which leads to the heart.

The face drains mainly through the **facial vein**, which begins near the inner corner of the eye. The scalp and outer face also drain into the **external jugular vein**, which you can often see on the side of the neck when someone strains or sings.

Two kinds of connection link the outside to the inside:
- **Emissary veins** pass through small holes in the skull.
- The **ophthalmic veins** connect the face to the **cavernous sinus**.

These veins mostly lack one-way **valves**, so blood can flow either way. Example: an infected pimple on the nose or upper lip can spread to the cavernous sinus. That region is nicknamed the **danger triangle of the face**.
levels.college:
**Dural venous sinuses** are endothelium-lined spaces between the periosteal and meningeal layers of dura. They receive cerebral, diploic, meningeal and emissary veins, and they absorb CSF through arachnoid granulations.

Main route: **superior sagittal sinus** to the **confluence of sinuses** (torcula), then the **transverse sinus**, the **sigmoid sinus**, and the **internal jugular vein** at the jugular foramen. The inferior sagittal sinus joins the great cerebral vein (of Galen) to form the **straight sinus**, which also reaches the confluence. The **superior and inferior petrosal sinuses** drain the cavernous sinus, the superior into the transverse–sigmoid junction and the inferior into the IJV.

**Neck veins:**
- **IJV**: begins at the jugular bulb, runs in the carotid sheath lateral to the internal and common carotid arteries, and has the vagus nerve behind it. Its tributaries include the inferior petrosal sinus, facial, lingual, pharyngeal, and superior and middle thyroid veins.
- **External jugular vein (EJV)**: formed by the posterior auricular vein and the posterior division of the retromandibular vein. It crosses sternocleidomastoid superficially and enters the subclavian vein.
- **Retromandibular vein**: formed by the superficial temporal and maxillary veins inside the parotid. Its anterior division joins the facial vein to form the common facial vein, which enters the IJV.

**Facial vein**: begins as the **angular vein**, which communicates with the **superior ophthalmic vein** and so with the cavernous sinus. It also connects to the **pterygoid plexus** through the deep facial vein, and the plexus reaches the cavernous sinus through emissary veins in the foramen ovale.

**Emissary veins** (mostly valveless):
- Parietal, joining the scalp to the superior sagittal sinus
- Mastoid, joining the occipital or posterior auricular vein to the sigmoid sinus
- Condylar, joining the sigmoid sinus to the suboccipital plexus
- Veins through the foramen ovale and the foramen of Vesalius (sphenoidal emissary foramen)

These routes explain septic cavernous sinus thrombosis and how scalp infection can reach the meninges.
levels.phd:
The classic idea that facial veins are "valveless" is an oversimplification. Zhang and Stringer (2010) dissected facial veins and found valves in many specimens. Even so, flow across the angular–ophthalmic route is bidirectional and depends on pressure. The key point is that **pressure gradients**, not valves, decide which way blood moves. Anastomotic channels therefore act as overflow routes.

**Posture shifts outflow.** Lying supine, most cerebral drainage goes through the IJVs. When upright, the IJVs collapse because intraluminal pressure falls below atmospheric pressure. Drainage then shifts to the **vertebral venous plexus** and the condylar emissary pathways (Valdueza et al.; Gisolf et al. 2004). The valveless **Batson plexus** joins the intracranial sinuses to the epidural vertebral veins, and it also offers a route for metastatic spread.

**Sinus anatomy varies.** The confluence is asymmetric in most people, and the right transverse sinus is usually dominant, draining the superior sagittal sinus. Transverse sinus hypoplasia or aplasia is common. This matters when interpreting MR venography, because hypoplasia can look like thrombosis, and when planning surgery.

**Mastoid emissary veins** vary greatly in size. A large one can become a significant outflow route when a sigmoid sinus is occluded. **Diploic veins** (frontal, anterior and posterior temporal, occipital) run within the cancellous bone between the inner and outer tables. They link the scalp, emissary and sinus systems.

**Emissary veins as thermoregulators.** Cabanac and Brinnel proposed that emissary veins carry blood cooled at the scalp and face into the cranium, giving selective brain cooling during hyperthermia. The evidence in humans is debated.

**IJV variation.** Usually the right IJV is larger, continuing the dominant sigmoid sinus. A high-riding jugular bulb can sit in the middle ear and become exposed, which matters in otologic surgery. Valves near the IJV terminus help prevent backflow toward the brain. When these valves are incompetent, transient global amnesia and cough-related phenomena have been linked to retrograde jugular flow, though the cause is unproven.
levels.expert:
Clinical consequences arise from venous outflow, its pressure, and its connections to other compartments.

**Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST)** often presents subtly, with headache, papilledema, seizures, or hemorrhagic venous infarcts that do not follow arterial territories. Bilateral thalamic oedema suggests occlusion of the deep system (straight sinus or vein of Galen). Imaging pitfalls include arachnoid granulations and hypoplastic sinuses that mimic filling defects, while the "empty delta" sign on contrast CT is a genuine sign of sinus thrombosis. Treatment is anticoagulation, even when there is hemorrhage. Vaccine-induced immune thrombotic thrombocytopenia (VITT, 2021) showed that some CVST is immune-mediated through anti-PF4 antibodies, which changes the choice of anticoagulant.

**Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH)**: bilateral transverse sinus stenosis is seen in most patients, and a pressure gradient across it can be measured by venous manometry. Venous sinus stenting can lower pressure in selected patients. Whether stenosis causes IIH or results from it, by collapse under raised pressure, is still unresolved. **Pulsatile tinnitus** can come from sigmoid sinus diverticulum or dehiscence, or from a dural arteriovenous fistula. These deserve investigation.

**Neurosurgical implications:**
- During a retrosigmoid craniotomy, the mastoid emissary vein is a source of bleeding and of air embolism. Bone wax and careful positioning reduce the risk. Sitting-position surgery raises the risk of venous air embolism because the sinuses are under negative pressure.
- Sacrificing the superior sagittal sinus is usually tolerated in its anterior third but risky behind the coronal suture. The vein of Labbé and the bridging veins must be preserved to avoid venous infarction.
- Before ligating a sinus or performing jugular surgery, confirm contralateral outflow. Bilateral IJV ligation can raise intracranial pressure and cause facial oedema.

**Septic thrombophlebitis**: Lemierre syndrome, usually caused by *Fusobacterium necrophorum*, spreads from the pharynx to the IJV. Otogenic sigmoid sinus thrombosis follows mastoiditis. Septic cavernous sinus thrombosis, now rare thanks to antibiotics, causes ophthalmoplegia and chemosis.

Open questions include the role of the glymphatic and venous systems in outflow, and how jugular flow changes in microgravity. Spaceflight venous stasis and IJV thrombi have been documented in astronauts.

keyPoints: Dural sinuses drain via transverse and sigmoid sinuses into the internal jugular vein
The IJV exits through the jugular foramen and runs in the carotid sheath
The facial vein begins as the angular vein, linked to the superior ophthalmic vein
Emissary veins cross the skull to link scalp veins with the dural sinuses
Bidirectional flow explains the face's danger triangle and cavernous sinus thrombosis
Upright posture shifts outflow from the IJVs to the vertebral venous plexus

test.q: Through which opening does the internal jugular vein leave the skull?
test.explain: The sigmoid sinus becomes the IJV at the jugular foramen. The foramen ovale carries V3 and some emissary veins.

test.q: Which sinus continues directly into the internal jugular vein?
test.explain: The transverse sinus leads into the sigmoid sinus, which becomes the IJV.

test.q: The facial vein begins near the eye as which vein?
test.explain: The angular vein at the medial eye becomes the facial vein and connects to the superior ophthalmic vein.

test.q: Why can a nose infection reach the cavernous sinus?
choices: Arteries carry germs straight to the brain
Nerves of the nose pass through the sinus
Lymph from the nose drains into the sinus
Facial and ophthalmic veins allow two-way flow
test.explain: Facial veins connect to the cavernous sinus through the ophthalmic veins, and flow can go either way. Arteries and lymph are not the route.

test.q: The retromandibular vein is formed by which pair of veins?
test.explain: It forms in the parotid from the superficial temporal and maxillary veins.

test.q: Which structure lies inside the carotid sheath alongside the IJV?
test.explain: The carotid sheath holds the carotid artery, the IJV and the vagus nerve, which runs behind them.

test.q: The great cerebral vein joins the inferior sagittal sinus to form the:
test.explain: The vein of Galen and the inferior sagittal sinus unite as the straight sinus, which drains to the confluence.

test.q: The pterygoid plexus reaches the cavernous sinus partly through veins in the:
test.explain: Emissary veins through the foramen ovale (and the foramen of Vesalius) link the plexus to the cavernous sinus.

test.q: Into which vein does the external jugular vein usually drain?
test.explain: The EJV crosses sternocleidomastoid and empties into the subclavian vein.

test.q: Veins passing through skull foramina to link scalp veins with dural sinuses are called ___ veins.
test.explain: Emissary veins connect veins outside the skull with the sinuses inside it.

test.q: What nickname is given to the area around the nose and upper lip, where infections can spread to the cavernous sinus?
test.explain: Bidirectional venous flow through the angular and ophthalmic veins makes this area risky.

test.q: The place where the superior sagittal, straight and transverse sinuses meet is the ___ of sinuses.
test.explain: The confluence of sinuses, also called the torcula, sits at the internal occipital protuberance.

kidTest.q: What do veins do?
choices: Carry blood back to the heart
kidTest.explain: Veins bring used blood back home to the heart.

kidTest.q: What is the biggest vein leaving the head?
kidTest.explain: The jugular vein in the neck carries most blood out of the head.

kidTest.q: What are the blood tunnels inside the skull called?
kidTest.explain: Sinuses are tunnels in the tough covering around the brain.

kidTest.q: Why should a pimple near the nose be watched?
choices: It can make your nose grow longer
It stops your eyes from blinking
Germs can travel inside through veins
kidTest.explain: Face veins connect to the tunnels inside the skull, so germs can travel.

kidTest.q: Tiny veins that poke through skull holes are e _ _ _ _ _ _ _ veins.
kidTest.explain: Emissary veins link the outside and the inside of the skull.

advancedTest.q: A patient stands up. What happens to cerebral venous outflow?
choices: Outflow shifts toward the vertebral venous plexus
The dural sinuses collapse and outflow stops
The jugular veins widen and carry more of the outflow
Outflow reverses into the facial veins
advancedTest.explain: When upright, the IJVs collapse under sub-atmospheric pressure, so the vertebral plexus and condylar routes take over.

advancedTest.q: MR venography shows absent flow in the left transverse sinus of a well patient. What is the best caution?
choices: Hypoplasia is common and can mimic thrombosis
This finding proves idiopathic intracranial hypertension
Left-sided sinuses are dominant, so this is urgent
Diagnose thrombosis and start treatment at once
advancedTest.explain: The transverse sinuses are often asymmetric, and hypoplasia, usually on the left, can imitate occlusion.

advancedTest.q: Before ligating the right sigmoid sinus, what matters most to confirm?
choices: Size of the facial vein on that side
Patency of the external carotid artery
Competence of the angular vein valves
advancedTest.explain: Losing a dominant outflow route without adequate drainage on the other side risks venous hypertension and infarction.

advancedTest.q: Why is the debate about transverse stenosis in IIH unresolved?
choices: Manometry is unable to measure sinus gradients
Stenting has failed to lower pressure in trials
Stenosis is rarely seen on imaging in IIH
High pressure may cause stenosis, or vice versa
advancedTest.explain: Raised pressure can compress a sinus, and a stenosed sinus can raise pressure, so cause and effect are uncertain. Stenting does lower pressure in selected patients, and stenosis is seen in most.
